books.section: Topic 5.9 Government Policies During the Civil War
Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: Abraham Lincoln, Emancipation Proclamation, January 1, 1863. Public domain. Wording verified against the Avalon Project text. Leading “...” marks the omitted opening of the quoted sentence; “. . .” marks omitted text between passages, quoted in their order in the source.
stimulus.text:
“... And by virtue of the power, and for the purpose aforesaid, I do order and declare that all persons held as slaves within said designated States, and parts of States, are, and henceforward shall be free; and that the Executive government of the United States, including the military and naval authorities thereof, will recognize and maintain the freedom of said persons. . . . And I further declare and make known, that such persons of suitable condition, will be received into the armed service of the United States to garrison forts, positions, stations, and other places, and to man vessels of all sorts in said service. . . . And upon this act, sincerely believed to be an act of justice, warranted by the Constitution, upon military necessity, I invoke the considerate judgment of mankind, and the gracious favor of Almighty God.”

—Abraham Lincoln, Emancipation Proclamation, January 1, 1863

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: By freeing enslaved people in rebel territory and inviting them into Union service, the proclamation most directly helped the Union

options.text: win the border states’ support for the immediate abolition of slavery.
options.misconception: Background: the border states stayed slave states until the Thirteenth Amendment; the proclamation deliberately left them out.

options.text: end the violent draft riots that broke out in Northern cities in 1863.
options.misconception: Background: the draft riots came in July 1863, months after the proclamation, and were aimed at the draft, not at emancipation.

options.text: force the Confederacy to surrender at once, ending the war in 1863.
options.misconception: Background: the Confederacy fought on for more than two years after the proclamation, until April 1865.

options.text: keep Britain and France from aiding the Confederacy, since neither could openly back slavery.

rationales.A: Background: the border states stayed slave states until the Thirteenth Amendment; the proclamation deliberately left them out.
rationales.B: Background: the draft riots came in July 1863, months after the proclamation, and were aimed at the draft, not at emancipation.
rationales.C: Background: the Confederacy fought on for more than two years after the proclamation, until April 1865.
rationales.D: Once the Union fought openly against slavery, Britain and France could not aid the Confederacy without seeming to defend slavery, so the proclamation shut the door on foreign help.
rationales.general:
1. Before 1863 the war looked like a quarrel over union, and Europe could side with the South for cotton.
2. The proclamation renames the war as a fight against slavery too.
3. Background: Britain had already ended slavery in its empire, and its public would not back a slaveholding cause.
4. A European government could not openly aid a rebellion that now stood for slavery.
Remember: renaming a war can close doors abroad that armies cannot reach.
